concept.name: Bull flag
concept.definition: A short-term continuation pattern consisting of a sharp near-vertical advance (the flagpole) followed by a brief, tight counter-trend consolidation in a small parallel channel sloping downward (the flag), typically lasting five to twenty bars. It is read as a pause that refreshes the uptrend, with continuation expected on a breakout above the flag's upper line. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: After a sudden surge, early buyers take profits in an orderly drift lower while new buyers absorb the supply; when the profit-taking is done, the trend resumes, often with similar force.
concept.mechanics: Identify the pole (sharp advance on rising volume) and the flag (a narrow parallel-channel pullback that should not retrace beyond roughly the midpoint of the pole, on declining volume). Entry is conventionally after a close above the flag's upper parallel line, with a stop below the flag's lower line. A common target adds the flagpole's height to the breakout point.
concept.formula: Price target = B + (T - F), where B = breakout price above the flag's upper line, T = top of the flagpole, and F = base of the flagpole.
concept.failure_modes: False breakouts are common when the flag drifts too deep (retracing more than half the pole) or too long, mutating into a full reversal; low-volume breakouts frequently fail. In choppy, trendless markets 'flags' appear constantly and mean little.
concept.misconceptions: That the flag's downward drift signals weakness — a controlled, low-volume pullback is precisely what defines the pattern; heavy-volume declines invalidate it. Also, flags have parallel channel lines; converging lines make it a pennant or wedge, not a flag.
concept.example: A stock jumps from $40 to $65 in days, then drifts down in a tight channel between $55 and $51 for two weeks on shrinking volume; a close above $55 projects a target near $80.
